def: The complete message a person sends Claude to request work: the instruction itself plus any background, examples, constraints and source material that come with it.
eg: Output quality tracks the quality of this message. Anything Claude needs and does not already have in the conversation has to be written into it or attached.

def: Information about the purpose of a task, the intended reader and the situation around it, supplied so Claude can aim its answer instead of guessing.
eg: Claude does not know your company, audience or goal unless told. Missing background is the most common reason for generic output.

def: Stating exactly what you want, in what form and under which limits, rather than hoping the model will infer it. Anthropic compares Claude to a brilliant new employee who lacks your norms and workflows.
eg: If you want extra effort or extra features, ask for them explicitly; vague requests get a minimal, middle-of-the-road result.

def: A quick self-check in which you imagine handing your request to a coworker who knows nothing about the task; if that person would be confused, Claude is likely to be confused too.
eg: Anthropic's prompting guide calls this its golden rule. It catches missing context and ambiguous wording before you send.

term: Explaining the reason for an instruction
def: Adding the purpose behind a rule, for example that the text will be read aloud by a speech tool, so Claude can apply the intent to cases the rule never mentioned.
eg: A bare 'never do X' gets followed narrowly; a rule with its reason generalizes better.

def: A direct statement of the shape the answer should take: a table with named columns, three bullet points, a 150-word email, or a numbered checklist.
eg: Without it Claude chooses a shape for you. Specifying one makes results easier to reuse, compare and paste elsewhere.

def: Explicit limits placed on a response, such as word count, reading level, tone, topics to avoid, or the sources it may rely on.
eg: Pair each limit with what you do want, and with the reason when it is not obvious.

def: Phrasing a requirement as the behavior you want ('write in flowing paragraphs') instead of a ban ('no bullet points'), which steers format and tone more reliably.
eg: Anthropic's formatting guidance lists this first: tell Claude what to do instead of what not to do.

def: Including a handful of sample inputs paired with the outputs you want, so Claude copies the pattern of format, tone and structure. One example is a fine start; three to five well-chosen ones are recommended.
eg: Good examples are relevant to the real task, diverse enough to cover edge cases, and clearly separated from the instructions.

def: Visible dividers or tags, such as putting a pasted email between a line reading 'begin pasted email' and one reading 'end pasted email', that separate instructions from source material and from each other so nothing is misread.
eg: They matter most when a request mixes instructions, documents, examples and data. Consistent, descriptive labels work; plain headings can serve the same purpose.

def: Telling Claude to take a specific viewpoint, such as a skeptical finance reviewer, so tone and priorities follow that vantage point. Saying what the perspective cares about works better than a bare job title.
eg: Anthropic's prompting advice treats it as optional; being explicit about the perspective you want works better than a grand title.

def: A layout for prompts with long pasted material: the source text goes near the top and the actual question or task follows it, which Anthropic's tests found can improve response quality.
eg: Long-context prompts usually fare better when the ask comes after the material, and when each document is labeled.

def: Splitting a large, multi-part job into smaller steps in a clear order, each with a single purpose, so every piece gets full attention and can be checked on its own.
eg: A single overloaded request tends to produce a muddled blend. Decompose when stages need different instructions or you want checkpoints.

def: Running a series of requests in which each answer becomes the input to the next, for example extract the facts, then analyze them, then draft the summary, so you can inspect and fix the intermediate results.
eg: Anthropic notes it trades speed for accuracy. Keep each link to one job done well.

def: A three-step sequence: produce a draft, have Claude assess it against criteria you state, then revise the draft using that assessment.
eg: Each step can be reviewed or branched. The review is only as good as the criteria you provide, and it does not replace checking facts.

def: Listing the actions Claude should take as numbered steps when order or completeness matters, such as 'first extract dates, then flag conflicts, then draft the recap'.
eg: Numbered steps make skipped work visible and give you a handle for feedback ('step 3 was too long').

def: Treating the first answer as a draft: review it, name the specific gap, adjust the request or give targeted feedback, and run it again until the output meets the standard.
eg: First prompts rarely land perfectly. Change one thing at a time so you know what helped.

def: A follow-up message that says exactly what to keep and what to change ('keep the dates, cut to 150 words, warmer tone'), rather than a bare 'try again' or 'make it better'.
eg: Specific feedback converges quickly; vague feedback makes Claude guess which part you disliked.

def: Starting with a short, plain request and adding rules or techniques only when a specific shortfall calls for them, checking that each addition actually helps.
eg: Prompts that grow by accretion become long and self-contradictory. Add structure to fix an observed problem, not by habit.

def: A definition, written before you start, of what a good result looks like (coverage, format, accuracy bar, intended reader) that lets you judge an output and steer the request.
eg: Without it, 'better' is a matter of mood. Criteria also feed review steps and make research requests focused.

def: Inviting Claude to ask what it needs to know before it starts, useful when a request has missing details or several reasonable interpretations.
eg: A few minutes of questions up front beats rounds of rework on a draft that guessed the wrong audience.

def: Asking Claude to work through a multi-part problem in stages before giving its answer, which tends to help with logic, math and constraint-heavy tasks. Extended thinking, where available, is generally the stronger route.
eg: Useful for scheduling puzzles, budgets and multi-condition rules. Still check the result.

def: A reusable request with fixed instructions and placeholders for the parts that change each time, such as [report] or [audience], so recurring tasks stay consistent between people and weeks.
eg: Templates capture what already worked. Store them somewhere shared; update them when you learn a better wording.

def: Adapting a request to data work: supply the data, state the question to answer, ask Claude to show its method and assumptions, and specify the figures or tables you need.
eg: A bare 'what do you think of this data?' invites a vague tour. Naming metrics and the decision the numbers support sharpens it.

def: Asking for a sourced investigation: state what a successful answer must cover, ask Claude to cross-check across several sources and flag conflicts or gaps, and request the links.
eg: Anthropic's research guidance names clear success criteria and source verification as the first two steps.

def: Writing requests that name the reader, purpose, tone and length and show samples of the voice you want, then refine the draft in rounds.
eg: Describing a voice with adjectives alone is weaker than pasting two real examples of it.

def: Idea-generation requests that ask for many varied options, deliberately different in angle, before judging any of them, then narrow with criteria in a follow-up.
eg: Asking for 'the best idea' up front collapses variety. Separate generating from choosing.

def: Adding documents or images to a chat so Claude works from the actual material. Supported types include PDF, Word, spreadsheets, text and common image formats; the request should still say what to do with them.
eg: Say which file and which part you mean. When pointing to PDF pages, use the page numbers your viewer shows.

term: PDF page limit for visual analysis
def: The Help Center rule that Claude reads both the text and visual elements such as charts only for PDFs up to 100 pages; longer ones are processed as text only.
eg: If a chart in a long report matters, split out the relevant pages or paste the chart as an image.

def: Asking for help with a formula, script or software fault by supplying the exact error message, the tool and its version, representative input and the result you expected.
eg: Claude can only diagnose what it can see. Complex implementations are escalated to developers rather than improvised in chat.

def: How non-PDF files such as Word documents are processed: Claude pulls out the text, and images embedded in the file cannot be read.
eg: If a diagram inside a document matters, take a screenshot and attach it as an image.

def: A fluent, confident statement from a language model that is false or unsupported, such as an invented statistic, quotation, source or legal citation.
eg: Even strong models do it. Techniques reduce it but do not eliminate it, so validate anything that matters.

def: A reference that looks real (author, year, case name, section number, link) but points to nothing, or does not say what Claude claims it says.
eg: Specific-looking detail is not evidence. Open the source and confirm it exists and supports the point before the citation travels.

def: A rating or reassurance Claude gives about how sure it is of its own answer, which is not independent evidence that the answer is correct.
eg: Asking 'are you sure?' or 'rate your confidence' is not verification. Check against an outside source instead.

def: The point after which a model's training data stops, so later events, prices, laws and product releases are unknown to it unless search or supplied documents provide them.
eg: Questions about 'current' anything need web search or an attached source, and the answer still needs checking.

def: A failure in which Claude says it sent an email, saved a file or produced a working link although no connected tool let it do so.
eg: Claude can only act through tools that are actually connected. Confirm outside actions in the real application.

def: A contradiction inside one output or across a conversation, such as two different totals for the same figure or a name that changes between sections.
eg: Long outputs drift. Scan figures, names and dates for agreement before sharing.

def: Judging whether each factual claim, number and quotation in an output is correct by comparing it with a reliable source.
eg: Distinct from completeness: a response can be entirely accurate and still leave out something the request needed.

def: Judging whether an output covers everything the request required, with no required topic, field or condition left out.
eg: A neat-looking answer can silently skip items, for example listing five action items from a transcript that contains nine.

def: A list, built from the original request, of every topic, field or condition the output must address, used to spot omissions quickly.
eg: Write it before you read the output so the answer's polish does not set your expectations.

def: The original document, dataset, regulation or publication a claim comes from, as opposed to a summary or retelling of it. It is the standard against which Claude's statement is checked.
eg: Verify a figure against the report it came from, not against another article that repeats it.

def: Confirming an important claim with a separate reliable source, or several, instead of accepting a single answer.
eg: Two answers from the same chat are not independent. Independence is what gives the check its value.

def: Opening the links Claude supplies with a web-search answer to confirm they exist, say what was claimed and are current. The Help Center advises reviewing them, since the original pages may hold context that Claude's summary leaves out.
eg: Citations make checking possible; they do not make claims true. Original pages often contain context that a summary omits.

def: Assessing whether a source is authoritative, current and free of an angle, favoring primary documents and recognized institutions over anonymous or promotional pages.
eg: Search-based answers can lean on weak pages. Ask for primary sources and check publication dates.

def: Anchoring an answer in specific supplied or retrieved material, such as an attached document or search results, so that each claim can be traced back to it.
eg: Grounded answers can be checked against the material. Pair it with an instruction to say when the material does not contain the answer.

def: Asking Claude to pull word-for-word excerpts from a long document before it analyzes them, so the later reasoning rests on text that can be located and checked.
eg: Anthropic recommends this for long documents. If the quote cannot be found in the file, the claim built on it is suspect.

def: A follow-up step in which Claude finds a supporting passage for every claim in its own draft and removes or flags any claim it cannot support.
eg: It makes the output auditable. A person should still spot-check the passages it points to.

def: Telling Claude it may state that information is missing or that it is unsure, instead of filling gaps with plausible guesses. This simple instruction can sharply cut invented content.
eg: If a document might not contain the answer, write that possibility into the request.

def: Instructing Claude to answer only from the material you supplied and to say so when the answer is not there, rather than blending in what it remembers from training.
eg: Useful for policy, contract and report questions where only the document counts.

def: Running the same request several times and comparing the answers; claims that change from run to run are suspect and need checking.
eg: Agreement is not proof, since a model can repeat the same error, but disagreement is a useful warning.

def: When an answer looks wrong, reading the summary of Claude's thinking, or asking it to lay out its steps, to locate a faulty assumption or a logic slip.
eg: In the Claude apps the thinking summary can be expanded. It is a diagnostic aid, not a guarantee of correctness.

def: Asking Claude to critique its own draft against stated criteria and fix what it finds. It catches inconsistencies and gaps but is not a substitute for checking facts against outside sources.
eg: Useful as a first filter. The same blind spots that produced an error can survive its own review.

def: Verifying a random selection from a large output, such as 20 of 500 classified rows, plus the ambiguous cases, to estimate the error rate before trusting the rest.
eg: If the sample shows too many errors, improve the instructions and rerun rather than patching row by row.

def: Recomputing key figures with a spreadsheet formula, calculator or separate tool and comparing them with Claude's totals. The Help Center advises checking critical calculations with dedicated software or by hand.
eg: Do it for anything that feeds a decision or a report. Also confirm the inputs Claude used.

def: A quick reasonableness test on figures, such as the right order of magnitude, totals that add up, percentages that stay within bounds and dates in sequence, that exposes glaring errors fast.
eg: It will not catch subtle mistakes, but it is cheap and catches many of the embarrassing ones.

def: A systematic tilt in a response, such as stereotyped assumptions, one-sided framing, uneven treatment of groups or viewpoints, or important perspectives left out.
eg: Bias can sit in what is omitted or how a topic is framed, not only in explicit statements.

def: Sending the same request twice with one personal detail changed, such as a name, gender or region, and comparing the responses to reveal unequal treatment.
eg: A practical check for HR, hiring, lending and customer-communication drafts.

def: Asking for the strongest case on several sides of an issue, or for the main counterarguments, to counter one-sided framing.
eg: Pair it with a request for sources so each perspective can be checked.

def: A request whose wording presupposes the answer, such as 'Explain why this policy failed', which nudges the output toward the asker's assumption.
eg: Neutral phrasing ('summarize the evidence for and against') gets a fairer answer.

def: A tendency to agree with or flatter the user's stated view instead of giving an honest assessment.
eg: Counter it by asking for the strongest objections or for a critique, and do not read agreement as validation.

def: A workflow step in which a person reviews and approves Claude's output before it is used or sent, rather than letting it go out automatically.
eg: The more serious the consequences of an error, the more essential this step becomes.

def: Matching the depth of checking to the consequences of being wrong: a quick read for a brainstorm, a source-by-source check for a figure headed to a regulator.
eg: Checking everything equally wastes effort; checking nothing is how errors reach customers.

def: Content whose errors could cause legal, financial, medical, safety, regulatory or reputational harm, or could affect an individual's job or access to services.
eg: Qualified human review is expected before anything in this class is relied on or sent.

def: Having someone with real expertise in the field, such as legal counsel, an accountant or a clinician, check content in their area before it is relied on.
eg: Claude can draft and organize; accountable professionals sign off where professional judgment is required.

def: The human tendency to accept an automated system's output without scrutiny because it looks authoritative and polished.
eg: Polish and confidence are the very signals that lower a reader's guard. Build review habits to counter it.

def: Rewriting the same underlying content for a different reader by changing depth, vocabulary, length, tone and lead point without altering the facts.
eg: State the reader, the reason they are reading and what you want them to do, for example 'executives, decision needed, 150 words'.

def: The risk that shortening, simplifying or restyling a text quietly changes a number, qualifier or claim, so rewritten versions must be rechecked against the original.
eg: 'Approximately 12%' becoming 'about a tenth' may be fine; 'may' becoming 'will' is not.

def: An editing action: highlighting one passage of a draft and having Claude rewrite just that selection while everything else stays untouched.
eg: It protects text you have already approved and keeps iterations small and reviewable.

def: Producing two or three variants of the same piece and weighing them against stated criteria, such as tone, accuracy and length, before choosing or merging.
eg: Say what differs between variants ('formal, friendly, brief') so the comparison is meaningful.

term: Editing an earlier message to branch
def: Changing a message earlier in a chat to create a separate version of the conversation with its own artifacts, so another direction can be explored without losing the original path.
eg: A cheap way to compare approaches without muddying one long thread.

def: Selecting, sorting and trimming material into what a reader needs: removing duplicates and noise, grouping by theme, and keeping only items that serve the purpose.
eg: Give Claude the criteria for what to keep. Curation without criteria is arbitrary.

def: Combining several sources into one view that shows where they agree, where they conflict and what is missing, instead of summarizing each in turn.
eg: Ask for a comparison table of claims by source, with conflicts flagged, then verify the flagged items.

def: The choice between content that opens in its own window beside the chat as a saved, editable, shareable piece, typically self-contained and longer than about 15 lines, and a short answer left in the flow of the conversation.
eg: Quick answers and clarifications stay inline. Documents, tools and anything you will edit or reuse suit an artifact.

def: Output organized in fixed fields, such as table columns, CSV columns or JSON keys, so it can be sorted, filtered, imported or compared instead of read as flowing prose.
eg: Define the columns and the allowed values up front so every row is consistent.

def: Spreadsheets with working formulas, documents, slide decks and PDFs that Claude builds in a sandboxed environment when code execution and file creation is switched on.
eg: Generated files still need review before they are shared: formulas, numbers and wording can be wrong.

def: Confirming that figures and fields Claude pulled out of documents such as invoices or emails match the originals, including the column totals, before the data enters another system.
eg: Extraction is a common Claude task and a common place for silent errors, such as a misread digit.

def: Opening every URL that Claude supplies before sharing it, because Claude can generate links that do not work.
eg: The Help Center warns about broken links and about claims that a document was produced when it was not.

def: The principle that the person who sends or publishes Claude-assisted content remains responsible for its accuracy, however much of it Claude drafted.
eg: Claude is a drafting and analysis aid; the signature, the decision and the consequences stay with a person.

def: The fastest and lowest-priced Claude tier, suited to high-volume, latency-sensitive work such as classification, extraction and routing.
eg: Think quick, cheap and good enough for straightforward tasks. Not the pick when a task needs deep reasoning.

def: The middle Claude tier, described by Anthropic as the best combination of speed and intelligence, and a sensible default for everyday drafting, analysis and content work.
eg: When nothing in the scenario demands either the lowest cost or the deepest reasoning, this balanced tier is the usual starting point.

def: The high-capability Claude tier built for demanding, long-running knowledge work and complex reasoning, with moderate speed and a higher price than the smaller tiers.
eg: Reserve it for tasks where quality outweighs speed and cost, such as nuanced multi-document analysis.

def: A premium Claude tier positioned above Opus, Anthropic's most capable generally available model, aimed at demanding reasoning and long-horizon work; it is the slowest and most expensive.
eg: The exam guide names Haiku, Sonnet and Opus, but this newer top tier exists in the current lineup. Reach for it only when the next tier down still falls short.

def: The basic tension in model choice: the more capable models are generally slower and more expensive, so each task is matched to the lightest option that still meets the quality bar.
eg: Using the top model for every job wastes budget and time; using the smallest for hard reasoning wastes the output.

def: Starting with the smaller, cheaper model, testing it against your quality criteria, and moving up a tier or effort level only where it falls short.
eg: Anthropic's model-choice guide lists it as the right starting point for prototyping, high-volume and cost-sensitive work.

def: Starting with the strongest option for tasks where accuracy outweighs cost, then trimming toward lighter models or lower effort as you learn what the task really needs.
eg: Fits complex reasoning and high-stakes analysis. The cost is paid up front, then optimized.

def: Using a lighter model for bulk or early-stage work such as first drafts and sorting, and a stronger one for the final judgment or polish.
eg: In the Claude apps you can switch models between messages, so a workflow can use each tier where it earns its cost.

def: The menu beside the send button in the Claude apps that shows the current model and effort setting and lets you switch; a change takes effect with Claude's next response.
eg: Switching mid-conversation is allowed, which makes it easy to try a stronger model on a hard step.

def: A Claude setting from low through medium, high and extra high to max that controls how thoroughly Claude works; higher settings give more thorough answers but take longer and use limits faster.
eg: Anthropic notes that tuning this is often a better lever than switching models. Lower settings suit routine tasks.

def: A mode in which Claude reasons through a hard problem before replying, trading time for better results on math, logic and multi-angle analysis. It does not fetch new information.
eg: In the Claude apps it appears as a Thinking control separate from effort. Wrong tool for 'what happened this week'.

def: A feature that lets Claude pull current information from the live web and cite it, best for quick factual lookups that take one or two searches.
eg: Answers include source links you should open. For multi-source investigations, step up to the research mode.

def: A mode for in-depth investigation in which Claude runs many connected searches across the web and your enabled integrations, then returns a longer cited report; it takes minutes, needs web search and is limited to paid plans.
eg: Choose it for comparisons, landscape reviews and updating documents with web facts. It uses your limits faster than ordinary chat.

def: The default back-and-forth conversation with Claude, suited to quick questions, drafting and iteration where no persistent files or special mode is needed.
eg: Most one-off work belongs here. Escalate to a Project, research or an artifact only when the task calls for it.

def: The product choice between a workspace that keeps shared files, instructions and related conversations together for recurring work, and a single conversation that starts from scratch and suits a one-off question.
eg: If you keep re-pasting the same brief, guidelines or reference files, that is the signal to build a Project.

def: The total amount of text Claude can consider at once in a conversation, covering your messages, its replies, attached files and standing instructions; it works like short-term working memory and is counted in tokens.
eg: It is different from the model's training data. A thread that outgrows it has to be summarized or restarted.

def: The small unit of text, a word fragment, a short word or a punctuation mark, that a model reads and counts; context limits and usage are measured in these.
eg: Longer prompts, big attachments and long replies all consume them, so they connect to speed, cost and limits.

def: The decline in accuracy and recall as more and more material piles into a conversation, so a larger window does not mean everything inside it is used equally well.
eg: Curating what is in context matters as much as how much fits. Send the relevant sections, not the whole archive.

def: A paid-plan behavior, available when code execution is enabled, in which Claude summarizes earlier messages as a conversation nears its limit so it can keep going; the full history is kept, but long chats use more of your allowance.
eg: It stretches a conversation but does not make a sprawling thread a good place to work.

def: Opening a fresh chat when a thread has drifted across topics, piled up contradictory instructions or grown so long that early details slip, while carrying forward only what still matters.
eg: A fresh start with a clean brief usually beats arguing with a cluttered thread.

def: A short recap Claude writes of the decisions made, requirements and open questions in a long conversation, which you check and paste into a new chat to continue cleanly.
eg: Review it for errors before reuse; whatever the summary gets wrong will be inherited by the new chat.

def: Keeping stable reference material and standing guidance somewhere durable, such as Project files and instructions or memory, instead of re-pasting it into every new conversation.
eg: Decide per item: what is stable goes in a durable home, what is specific to today's task goes in the chat.

def: A Claude setting that saves useful details from your conversations, such as your role and ongoing projects, as editable topics and draws on them in later chats; it can be viewed, edited, paused or turned off.
eg: Helpful for continuity; for one-off or unrelated tasks it can carry in unwanted background.

def: A paid-plan feature in which Claude searches your earlier conversations when asked, shows each lookup as a tool call and cites the chats it used.
eg: Searches stay within a Project's own chats or within non-Project chats, and incognito chats are never searched.

def: Memory kept separately for each Project so work for one client or topic does not bleed into another; account-level memory can be switched off for a Project to isolate it fully.
eg: Inside a Project Claude uses that Project's memory plus account memory, never another Project's.

def: A toggle in the plus menu, available only before the first message, that stops Claude from using or saving memory for that conversation.
eg: It cannot be changed once the chat has started, so decide up front for sensitive or unrelated tasks.

def: The plan allowance that every conversation draws from, consumed faster by long chats, higher effort, research and file creation.
eg: If limits run out quickly, check whether routine tasks are running at heavy settings.

def: Capabilities such as research, search of past chats and project retrieval that are offered only on certain plans or that an organization's administrators can switch off.
eg: Before designing a workflow around a feature, confirm your account actually has it.

def: How long you wait for a response, which grows with larger models, higher effort, extended thinking and research.
eg: Speed-sensitive, high-volume tasks should use lighter settings; deep analysis can afford to wait.

def: The work of establishing what a solution must do and within which limits, by reading stakeholder input such as interview notes, emails and tickets and separating firm needs from wishes, conflicts and gaps. Claude can organize and probe the input, but the people who own the need confirm the result.
eg: Ask Claude to name the source of each requirement and list the assumptions it made. A stakeholder still signs off.

def: Asking Claude to scan a brief or requirements document for statements that are vague, unmeasurable or open to more than one reading, such as 'fast' or 'user-friendly', and to propose measurable wording for people to confirm.
eg: Catching vague wording before work starts costs far less than discovering after a build that two teams read the same line differently.

def: A running list of the things a plan treats as true without proof, such as an expected volume or a system's availability, each with an owner who will confirm or challenge it.
eg: Claude can draft the list from a plan and ask what would change if each item proved false. People verify the items.

def: A one-sentence requirement written from the viewpoint of the person who needs it, in the pattern 'as a [role], I want [capability] so that [benefit]'.
eg: Claude can turn interview notes into draft stories quickly. The requester should read them back to confirm they say what was meant.

def: A comparison of how a process or capability works today against how it needs to work, listing what is missing between the two states.
eg: Give Claude both descriptions. It can only find gaps in what it has been told, so incomplete input produces an incomplete list.

def: The judgment of whether a task suits Claude, weighing how often it recurs, how much time it takes, how structured its inputs are, how costly an error would be and what data it touches.
eg: Frequent, text-heavy, checkable and low-consequence work is a strong fit. High-stakes decisions about people and tasks needing restricted data are not.

def: Ranking candidate improvements by the benefit each promises against the work, risk and cost to deliver it, so that high-benefit, low-effort items go first.
eg: Claude can score a long idea list against criteria you supply. The team, not Claude, sets the weights and makes the call.

def: Writing out how work actually flows, step by step, with the owner, input and output of each step, so that delays, handoffs and rework become visible.
eg: Claude can turn a rambling description into a numbered step list or a diagram. Check it against how the work really happens.

def: The step in a process that limits how much work can finish in a given time, because items queue up in front of it.
eg: Speeding up any other step does not raise output. Claude can suggest candidates from a description, but timing data confirms which step it really is.

def: Improving a process by removing waiting time, rework, duplicate entry and needless approvals, with Claude proposing changes from a description and people testing them in practice.
eg: Target the measured constraint, change one step at a time and compare against the baseline.

def: A tree that splits a project into deliverables and then into tasks small enough to assign and estimate. Claude can propose a first version from a goal and constraints.
eg: Check for missing tasks and wrong dependencies. Claude does not know your team's real capacity unless you say so.

def: A log of what could go wrong with a project or rollout, each entry carrying a likelihood, an impact, an owner and a planned response.
eg: Claude is good at brainstorming risks across categories. People rate them and own the responses.

def: A planning exercise in which the team assumes a project has already failed and works backward to list the reasons, so weaknesses surface before launch.
eg: Ask Claude to imagine the failure and generate causes by category. The team then ranks them and plans mitigations.

def: A table that scores each option against weighted criteria so the choice between them can be traced and explained.
eg: Claude can suggest criteria and draft scores, but the weights express the organization's priorities and must be set by people.

def: A rough, working version of a tool, document or workflow built quickly so users can react to it before anyone invests in a full solution. In Claude it is often an interactive artifact.
eg: Build one to learn what users need. Anything that must connect to company systems or run at scale moves to specialists.

def: The cycle of putting a draft or workflow in front of its users, collecting what worked and what did not, and building that into the next version.
eg: Short loops with real users beat long design phases. Record each round's changes so you can see what improved results.

def: A way of working in which a person and Claude collaborate as thinking partners, going back and forth while the person keeps direction and judgment. It is one of three modes of AI interaction in Anthropic's AI Fluency framework.
eg: Most Associate-level work looks like this: brainstorming, drafting, analysis and review, with a human deciding.

def: A way of working in which Claude carries out a specific, well-defined task exactly as a person instructs, such as reformatting a stack of records the same way. It is one of three modes of AI interaction in Anthropic's AI Fluency framework.
eg: The person specifies the task and Claude executes it. Suits repetitive, rule-like work whose output is easy to check.

def: A way of working in which a person configures Claude in advance to carry out future tasks independently on their behalf. It is one of three modes of AI interaction in Anthropic's AI Fluency framework and calls for the clearest limits, permissions and oversight.
eg: More independence means more setup: define what it may do, what needs approval and how its work will be reviewed.

def: The competency of setting goals and deciding whether, when and how to bring AI into a piece of work, based on the task, the tool's strengths and the risks involved.
eg: Anthropic's framework pairs it with Description, Discernment and Diligence. Good delegation starts before any prompt is written.

def: Rethinking the order, handoffs and roles in a process so that Claude's strengths are built in from the start, instead of adding Claude as an extra step on top of the old design.
eg: Choose it when the old process exists only because of old limits, such as retyping notes by hand. Otherwise a lighter addition carries less risk.

def: The exact step in an existing process where Claude is inserted, defined by what goes in, what comes out and who receives the result.
eg: Pick a step that is repetitive, text-heavy and easy to check, and keep a person where errors would be costly.

def: A three-stage workflow in which Claude produces a first version, a responsible person edits and checks it, and only then is it approved and released.
eg: The standard shape of an augmented workflow. The review stage is where accuracy, tone and policy are enforced; skipping it turns assistance into unchecked automation.

def: A written, step-by-step description of how a recurring task is done, which for a Claude-assisted task states the inputs, the instructions or template used, who reviews the output and what to do when something fails.
eg: Writing it down lets colleagues repeat the workflow and keeps it alive when its builder moves on.

def: A small, time-limited trial of a new Claude workflow with a limited group, run to measure results and find problems before a wider rollout.
eg: Agree the success measures before it starts and compare against the baseline you recorded.

def: Recording how long a task takes, what it costs and how often it needs correction before Claude is introduced, so that any improvement can be shown with evidence.
eg: Without one, 'it feels faster' is the only claim available, and stakeholders discount it.

def: A short, evidence-backed argument to stakeholders for using Claude on a process, stating the measured benefit, the cost, the known limits and the human review that remains.
eg: Lead with measured pilot results. Including the limitations builds credibility instead of weakening the case.

def: Telling stakeholders in advance what Claude does well, where it makes mistakes and which checks stay with people, so nobody treats its output as automatically correct.
eg: Overpromising is the fastest route to lost trust after the first visible error.

def: The chance that a workflow gets built but not used, because staff distrust its output, lack training, or find it slower or more awkward than their old method.
eg: Technical success does not guarantee use. Ask users what is blocking them and fix training or workflow before adding features.

def: The planned work of preparing people for a new way of working: communication, training, support channels, feedback and a named owner.
eg: Rolling out Claude is as much about people as tools. Plan it alongside the technical setup.

def: Widening the scope and independence given to an AI helper in stages as it proves reliable, instead of granting broad freedom on day one. It is named as one of four principles in Anthropic's course material on human-agent teams.
eg: Start with one team and tightly reviewed outputs. Relax checks only where results justify it.

def: Handing a request to Claude Developers or Architects when it needs system integration, custom code, automation at scale, security design or an enterprise rollout, which Associates are not expected to design themselves.
eg: Recognizing the limit of your own scope is itself a tested skill. Bring specialists a clear problem statement, the data involved and your prototype.

def: The files, documents and text stored in a Project that Claude can draw on in every chat inside that Project, so the background does not have to be pasted again.
eg: It supplies facts and reference material. Rules about behavior belong in instructions. On paid plans a very large collection switches on retrieval automatically.

def: Standing directions saved in a Project that apply to every chat in that Project and to no other, such as role, audience, tone, output format and what to do when information is missing.
eg: Use them for how Claude should behave. They do not follow you into chats outside the Project; account-wide instructions do that.

def: A setting, labeled 'Instructions for Claude' in the account's Settings, where general guidance such as preferred terminology and communication style is saved so that it is applied to all of a person's conversations.
eg: Keep it to preferences that are true everywhere. Client- or task-specific rules belong in a Project or a skill.

def: The split inside a Project between guidance on how Claude should behave and the reference material it should draw on: rules of conduct are saved in one place, documents and facts in the other.
eg: Burying rules inside a long document, or pasting documents into the rules, makes both harder to maintain and to find.

def: Standing instructions placed ahead of the conversation that define Claude's role, tone, rules and limits for everything that follows. In the Claude apps, the closest everyday equivalent is Project instructions.
eg: The blueprint's 'system-level instructions' refers to this standing layer, as opposed to the individual messages a person types.

def: The part of an instruction set that says what Claude is acting as, who will read its output and what that reader already knows, so that tone and depth are pitched correctly.
eg: A concrete statement ('you draft replies for retail customers who are not technical') beats a grand job title.

def: An instruction that says what Claude should do when it cannot complete a task as specified, for example when the knowledge does not hold the answer: say so plainly, ask a question, or route the request to a named person.
eg: Without one, Claude may fill the gap with a plausible guess. Pair it with a rule to quote the source whenever an answer exists.

def: One designated, maintained version of each piece of reference information, so that people and Claude never draw on conflicting copies.
eg: Before uploading a policy, confirm it is the current approved version and retire older copies from the Project.

def: Outdated documents left in a Project or connected source that Claude may still quote as though they were current.
eg: A Project does not expire its files. Someone has to remove or replace them when policies, prices or procedures change.

def: Giving each uploaded file a clear name that states its content and, where relevant, its date or version, such as 'Refund policy 2026-07', which helps Claude pick the right file and helps people spot outdated ones.
eg: The Help Center advises clear, descriptive filenames for retrieval. Names like 'final_v2_REAL' invite mix-ups.

def: A technique in which Claude searches a large body of material for the passages that matter to each question and answers from those, instead of holding everything in view at once. In Projects on paid plans it switches on automatically as stored knowledge nears the context limit and allows up to ten times more material.
eg: A visual indicator shows when it is active. Naming the specific document in your question and using clear filenames helps it find the right passages.

def: A link between Claude and an outside app or service, such as Google Drive, Gmail or Slack, through which Claude can search, read and in some cases act on that service for a person, within that person's permissions.
eg: Connectors are for live data and actions. They differ from uploaded files, which are static copies, and from skills, which carry procedures.

def: The connector that lets Claude search a person's Drive, read the Docs, Sheets, Slides and PDFs it finds there, and add selected Google Docs to chats and Projects. It reads text only, so images inside documents are not seen.
eg: Documents added this way stay in step with the live file. Adding them to a Project is limited to private Projects.

def: The connector that lets Claude search a person's email and answer questions from what it finds, citing the messages it used. It sees only the connected account's mail that the person can already open, and any action beyond reading is subject to that person's approval.
eg: Claude retrieves only the minimum needed for the request. Images embedded in emails and attachment contents are not read.

def: The rule that a connected service limits Claude to what the signed-in person can already see or do there; Claude cannot reach files, mailboxes or folders its user cannot open.
eg: If Claude cannot find a file, check the person's own access first. A custom connector that uses a shared credential is the exception: it reaches whatever that credential can.

def: The confirmation prompt that asks a person to approve before Claude carries out an action in a connected service, such as sending, sharing, moving or deleting something.
eg: Read what is about to happen before approving. Owners on Team and Enterprise plans decide whether members may let such actions run without asking each time.

def: The administrator step on Team and Enterprise plans in which an Owner adds a connector for the whole organization. It makes the connector available but does not by itself give anyone access to data.
eg: Each person must still sign in to the service with their own account, so access stays tied to individual permissions.

def: Owner-set controls that decide, for each category of connector action, whether Claude may act without asking, must ask first, or is blocked altogether. They can only narrow what the source system already allows.
eg: A typical split is reading allowed, writing and deleting needing approval. Restricting an action never grants more access than the service gives.

def: A packaged set of instructions, with optional scripts and reference files, that Claude loads on demand when a request matches it, giving repeatable procedures such as applying brand guidelines or a fixed report layout.
eg: Skills need code execution switched on and work across chats and Projects. Build one when you keep re-explaining the same format, tone and example.

def: The loading pattern in which Claude first sees only a skill's short name and description, and reads the full instructions and files only if the task needs them, which saves room in the context window.
eg: It is why many skills can be installed without crowding every conversation, and why the description decides whether a skill is used.

def: The short text in a skill that says what it does and when to use it, which Claude relies on to decide whether to load the skill for a given request.
eg: A vague one means the skill is ignored or fires at the wrong time. If a skill does not trigger, sharpen this first.

def: A single installable bundle that packages skills, connectors and related components for a role or team, so that people get a ready setup without configuring each piece.
eg: Organization Owners can distribute plugins to members. Install only from sources you trust.

def: The practice of adding skills, plugins and connectors only from publishers you trust and have reviewed, because they can carry instructions or code that put data at risk.
eg: The Help Center names prompt injection and data exfiltration as the main risks of an untrusted skill. Review bundled files first.

def: A periodic check of who and what has access, such as removing connectors that are no longer needed and ending shares of Projects that no longer need them.
eg: Access granted for a task tends to outlive the task unless someone looks. Disconnect services you no longer use.

def: The Team and Enterprise settings that decide whether a person added to a shared Project can only read it and chat in it, or can also change its instructions and knowledge.
eg: Give edit rights only to the people who maintain the Project; everyone else works from a stable configuration.

def: The named person accountable for a shared Project's or skill's instructions and files, who approves changes, reviews them on a schedule and tells users what changed.
eg: Shared configurations without an owner drift: files go stale, rules accumulate and nobody knows who may change them.

def: A simple record of each change made to a Project's instructions or files: what changed, who changed it, when and why.
eg: When behavior suddenly shifts, the log shows what changed so it can be reversed.

def: A small fixed collection of representative requests, with notes on what good answers look like, that is rerun after every change to instructions or knowledge to confirm that results did not get worse.
eg: A change that fixes one problem can quietly break another. Include a few tricky cases, not only easy ones.

def: A pre-configured project on Team and Enterprise plans, set up by an Owner, that searches an organization's connected tools such as documents, chat and email in one place and shows each person only what they are permitted to see.
eg: Results are permission-aware. Owners choose the connectors and each member signs in to their own accounts.

def: A Google Doc added to a chat or Project from Drive that remains linked to the live document, so Claude works from its current version rather than from a one-time copy.
eg: Editing the source changes what Claude sees. A file uploaded from disk is a static copy that someone must replace by hand.

def: A use of Claude that supports a person's own work, such as drafting, summarizing, brainstorming or analysis, where a human reviews the result and an imperfect output does little harm.
eg: The safest and most common place to start. Risk rises as output moves from informing a person to deciding about one.

def: A use in which Claude's output feeds advice or decisions that can significantly affect a person's rights, health, money or opportunities, such as legal, medical, credit, insurance, housing or employment matters.
eg: Anthropic's Usage Policy attaches extra requirements: a qualified person must meaningfully review the output, and the affected person must be told that AI was involved.

def: Examination of an AI recommendation by a qualified person who has the time, knowledge and authority to change or reject it, as opposed to a quick click-through that approves whatever appears.
eg: Anthropic's Usage Policy asks for review of this kind for high-risk recommendations, and the reviewer stays responsible for the outcome.

def: Reaching a decision about an individual, such as whether to hire, lend or grant a benefit, mainly from a system's output with little or no human judgment applied.
eg: Many laws and Anthropic's Usage Policy require human review and notice in these cases. Claude may inform the decision; a qualified person makes it.

def: Telling the people who receive or are affected by work, such as customers, applicants, patients or readers, that AI helped produce it.
eg: Anthropic's Usage Policy requires it for high-risk advice and for consumer-facing chatbots, and many employers and contracts add their own duty.

def: Material designed to mislead people about who produced it or whether it is genuine, such as fake reviews, invented testimonials, undisclosed fake personas or a bot posing as a human.
eg: Anthropic's Usage Policy prohibits these uses, and so do most corporate policies, however accurate the underlying claims might be.

def: Anthropic's published rules on what its products may not be used for and on the extra safeguards required for high-risk uses; it applies to everyone who uses Claude, on any plan.
eg: It sets the outer limit. An organization's own AI policy can be stricter, and cannot make a prohibited use acceptable.

def: The limit that Claude's answers on legal, medical, tax or investment questions are information to take to a qualified professional, not advice a person can rely on alone when deciding.
eg: Claude can help you prepare questions, summarize documents and explain terms. A licensed professional gives the advice and carries the responsibility.

def: Sorting information into tiers, such as public, internal, confidential and restricted, with rules for each tier about where and how it may be processed, including whether it may be given to an AI tool.
eg: Check the label before pasting or uploading. Policies usually allow public and some internal data in approved tools and forbid restricted data.

def: Information that identifies a specific person, alone or in combination, such as a name, email address, government ID number, account number or precise location.
eg: Remove, mask or replace it before sending data to Claude unless your policy and account explicitly allow it.

def: Health information tied to an identifiable individual that is handled by healthcare providers, insurers and their business partners and regulated in the United States under HIPAA.
eg: It may be processed only in tools covered by an appropriate agreement. Anthropic offers a Business Associate Agreement for HIPAA-ready commercial services, not for consumer plans.

def: Non-public information a company has a duty to protect, such as unreleased financials, strategy, source code, client data and trade secrets.
eg: Client contracts and employment agreements often limit where it may go. When unsure, treat it as restricted and ask.

def: Passwords, API keys, access tokens and similar values that unlock systems; they should never be typed into prompts, Project instructions, knowledge files or skills.
eg: The Help Center warns against hardcoding API keys or passwords in a skill. Use properly authenticated connections instead.

def: Giving Claude only the fields and records a task actually needs, and leaving out everything else, so that less sensitive data is exposed.
eg: To analyze overtime by department, send department and hours, not names and employee numbers.

def: Removing or blacking out sensitive details, such as names, numbers and addresses, from a document before it is shared with a tool.
eg: Check the result. Identifiers hide in headers, filenames, comments and tracked changes.

def: Stripping identifiers from data so thoroughly that individuals can no longer be identified, even by combining it with other information.
eg: Removing names is not always enough. Rare job titles, dates and locations can still point to a person.

def: Replacing identifiers with consistent codes or placeholders so that records can still be matched and analyzed, while the key linking codes back to people is kept separately and protected.
eg: It lowers risk, but the data may still count as personal data because the key allows re-identification.

def: The set of AI tools, plans and accounts that an organization has vetted for work use; anything outside it is not cleared for company data.
eg: Using Claude through the approved workspace rather than a personal account is often the difference between compliant and non-compliant use.

def: Use of AI tools or personal accounts for work without the knowledge or approval of IT, security or management, so company data flows where nobody has assessed the terms.
eg: Convenience is the usual cause. The remedy is to use approved tools or ask for the tool to be assessed, not to work around the policy.

def: The distinction between individual plans (Free, Pro, Max), where a model-improvement setting governs whether chats may be used to train models, and organizational plans and the API (Team, Enterprise, API), where inputs and outputs are not used for training by default.
eg: Know which applies to the account you are using before pasting anything sensitive. Company policies usually point to the organizational terms.

def: A privacy setting on individual Claude plans by which a person chooses whether their chats may be used to improve models. When it is on, data may be kept de-identified for up to five years; turning it off does not undo training that has already happened.
eg: Incognito chats are excluded even when it is on. The setting does not replace company policy on what data may be shared.

def: A conversation that is not saved to chat history or memory and is not used to improve Claude, even when the model-improvement setting is on.
eg: It does not change what an employer's policy allows, and on Team and Enterprise plans such chats still follow organizational retention.

def: How long conversations and files are kept before deletion, determined by plan, contract and administrator settings.
eg: Deleting a chat removes it from history at once, but deletion from back-end storage follows on a delay, so deleting is no way to undo sharing sensitive data. Enterprise Owners can set a custom period.

def: A contract that sets how a vendor may handle personal data on a customer's behalf. For Anthropic's commercial products it is incorporated automatically into the Commercial Terms.
eg: Privacy and legal teams look for one when assessing a vendor.

def: A contract that US health-privacy rules require before a vendor handles protected health information for a healthcare organization. Anthropic offers one for HIPAA-ready commercial services; consumer plans are not covered.
eg: Signing is necessary but not sufficient: use only the covered configuration and keep health data out of features marked as not covered.

def: The European Union law that governs how personal data of people in the EU is collected, used, stored and transferred, with duties such as a lawful basis, data minimization and honoring individuals' rights.
eg: Ask the privacy team before putting EU personal data into any new tool. A vendor's certifications do not make your own use lawful automatically.

def: An independent auditor's report on whether a service provider's security-related controls worked effectively over a period of time, often requested during vendor reviews.
eg: Anthropic lists SOC 2 Type I and Type II among its compliance credentials. A report supports a vendor review but does not decide your own regulatory obligations.

def: An international standard for an AI management system: the policies, roles and processes an organization uses to govern AI responsibly.
eg: Anthropic lists ISO/IEC 42001:2023 among its credentials. Read it as evidence of governance processes, not as a guarantee about any single output.

def: A structured review of a supplier's security, privacy, contract terms and track record before it is approved to handle company data.
eg: New AI add-ons, plugins and connectors may need one. Trying a tool with real data first is the wrong order.

def: A company document stating which AI tools, tasks and kinds of data staff may use, and what review, disclosure and record-keeping rules apply.
eg: When it conflicts with convenience, it wins. When it is silent on a situation, ask its owner instead of assuming permission.

def: The defined route for raising a concern about AI output, data exposure or a policy doubt to the right person, such as a manager, the privacy team or security, instead of handling it alone.
eg: Report promptly. A data mistake reported the same day is far easier to contain than one discovered later.

def: The roles, policies, approval steps and records through which an organization decides how AI may be used and checks that those decisions are followed.
eg: Associates meet it as rules about approved tools, data handling, review and disclosure, plus someone to ask.

def: A record of how AI contributed to a piece of work: which tool and account, when, for what purpose, who reviewed it and what was changed.
eg: Regulated teams often need it to explain a decision later. A short log entry now saves a reconstruction effort then.

def: A hidden or planted instruction inside a document, web page or message that tries to make Claude do something its user did not ask for, such as revealing information or taking an action.
eg: Treat files and pages from unknown sources with caution, keep sensitive connections out of such chats and stop Claude if it starts doing something unexpected.

def: A link that lets anyone who holds it read a snapshot of a conversation as it stood when shared; on Team and Enterprise plans it works only for members of the organization.
eg: Review the text before sharing, because the whole conversation is visible. Unsharing revokes the link.

def: Granting each person, connector or tool only the access it needs for the task, and no more.
eg: It applies to Project sharing, connector permissions and the data given to Claude, and it limits the damage from mistakes and misuse.

def: Machine-readable signals that can be added to what Claude produces, such as an invisible watermark in text and signed provenance metadata on supported files, so others can tell that Claude processed it.
eg: A detected mark is a signal, not proof, and a missing mark proves nothing: editing or conversion can remove marks, so 'no mark' never means 'written by a human'.

def: The competency of taking responsibility for what you do with AI and how you do it: choosing tools thoughtfully, being open about AI's role, and verifying work before it is shared.
eg: It is the responsible-use leg of Anthropic's framework, alongside Delegation, Description and Discernment.

def: A pattern in which a rule or tool that looks neutral still disadvantages people in a protected group, such as screening criteria that systematically filter out older or female applicants.
eg: AI-assisted screening and scoring can produce it without anyone intending bias. Compare outcomes by group and involve HR or legal before relying on it.

def: Working backward from what went wrong in an output, such as a bland answer, a wrong format or invented facts, to the most likely missing or faulty ingredient in the request or setup, before changing anything.
eg: Name the symptom, guess the cause, change one thing, retest. Random rewording wastes time.

def: A response that is technically on topic but bland and one-size-fits-all; the usual cause is missing context about the audience, the purpose, the situation and the standard of quality.
eg: Fix the request, not the reader: say who it is for, what it is for, and show an example of the voice you want.

def: A response whose shape is not what was needed, such as prose where a table was wanted; the usual cause is that no format was specified or that an example pointed somewhere else.
eg: State the format positively and show the layout, with named columns or a sample, rather than only forbidding the wrong one.

def: A requirement that Claude appears to have skipped, typically because it was buried in a long prompt, phrased only as a prohibition, or in conflict with another instruction.
eg: Make it prominent, state it positively, give the reason and check for contradictions before concluding that Claude 'won't listen'.

def: Two or more rules in the same prompt or instruction set that cannot both be satisfied, such as 'keep every answer to two sentences' alongside 'explain your reasoning in full'.
eg: Claude has to pick one, so results vary. Rewrite with priorities, for example brief by default and detailed on request.

def: Noticeably different outputs from repeated runs of the same request, most often because the request leaves format, definitions or criteria open for Claude to interpret.
eg: Stabilize with a fixed output layout, defined terms and a few examples. Structure matters more than clever wording.

def: A failure caused by Claude lacking the facts, such as private company data or events after its training cutoff, rather than by poor wording; rewording cannot fix it.
eg: Supply the material by attaching, connecting or searching, and ask Claude to answer only from it.

def: In a long conversation, the gradual slide away from rules or formats set early on, as newer material crowds them out.
eg: Restate the key rules, restart with a clean summary, or move standing rules into Project instructions so they apply to every chat.

def: Asking Claude to carry on a reply that stopped partway by supplying the original request and the part already produced, so it can pick up where it left off.
eg: The Help Center recommends giving Claude the previous prompt and response. Asking for the rest in sections avoids hitting the limit again.

def: The notice 'Your message will exceed the length limit for this chat', which means the input is too large for the conversation. The fixes are to split it, summarize key sections, have Claude identify the relevant parts, or start a new chat.
eg: On paid plans with code execution, older messages are summarized automatically, so this is rare. Retrying the same message changes nothing.

def: Cutting a long file into sections that fit within limits, processing each separately and then combining the results.
eg: Standard advice for 'file too large' problems. Ask Claude to keep a running list so nothing is lost between parts.

def: A reply in which Claude refuses or hedges. If the request was simply misread, stating the legitimate purpose and audience can help; if it conflicts with a policy, it is a limit to respect and not a puzzle to get around.
eg: Never disguise a request to slip past a boundary. Restate it plainly with context, or take the need to someone who can authorize it.

def: Disconnecting a connected service under Customize > Connectors and signing in to it again, to clear an access or authentication error such as a prompt to reconnect to Google Drive.
eg: If it still fails, the person's own access may have changed, or an administrator may need to approve the app.

def: Consulting Anthropic's public status page when Claude is erroring or unavailable for many users, to see whether a confirmed incident explains it before changing prompts or settings.
eg: A temporary 'capacity constraints' message reflects heavy demand, not a fault in your request: wait a few minutes and retry.

def: The underlying reason a problem occurs, as opposed to its visible symptom. Fixing it prevents repeats, whereas treating the symptom only hides it.
eg: Wrong totals may be a symptom; the cause may be a missing source file or an unclear definition. 'Be more careful' is rarely a fix.

def: Running two versions of a prompt on the same set of inputs and judging both against the same criteria, so the better one is chosen on evidence.
eg: Use identical inputs. Otherwise differences may come from the data and not from the wording.

def: Trying a prompt or workflow on unusual inputs, such as empty fields, odd formats, very long text or conflicting data, to find where it breaks before real use.
eg: A workflow that passes only on tidy samples will fail on the first messy file.

def: Keeping dated copies of each prompt or instruction version, with a note on what changed and how results moved, so that a version that worked can be restored.
eg: Without it, a 'fix' that made things worse cannot be undone with confidence.

def: Saving a prompt that finally produced the right result as a reusable template, Project instruction or skill, so that the success is repeatable by others.
eg: Do it at once, because the winning wording is easily lost in a long chat. Keep a sample of good output with it.

def: Replacing a failing method with a different one, such as another feature, a smaller step or a different source, after repeated tweaks to the same prompt have not helped.
eg: Examples: use web search for current facts, a Project for recurring context, or a human reviewer for judgment calls.

def: The point at which further tweaks to a prompt bring little or no improvement, signaling that the obstacle lies elsewhere, such as missing data, an unsuitable task or a need for technical help.
eg: Set a limit on iterations. When you reach it, change approach or escalate.

def: Grouping related questions or tasks into a single well-organized message instead of sending them one at a time, which saves usage and gives Claude the full picture.
eg: The Help Center lists it as a usage best practice. Do not mix unrelated topics, which muddles the answer.

def: Reused Project material that counts for less against usage limits while it is fresh, so many questions about the same documents cost fewer allowances; after a long break it counts in full again.
eg: A reason to keep recurring documents in a Project and to ask related questions together.

def: The share of Claude-assisted outputs that need substantial correction before they can be used, a measure of a workflow's quality.
eg: Time saved is only real if rework stays low. Track it alongside cycle time.

def: The elapsed time from starting a task to finishing it, including waiting and review, used to compare a workflow before and after Claude.
eg: Measure the whole loop. A fast draft followed by a long fix-up is not an improvement.

def: Removing human review or approval steps to gain speed, so that errors travel further before anyone sees them.
eg: Keep checkpoints where mistakes would be costly or hard to reverse. Relax them only where results justify it.
